name: Caldey
summary: Avalon's burying isle, which stood up when Morgana called: the strand before Caer Sidi, the haunted rowans and the burial lights, three of the witch's named, and Little Haven, the one corner the living hold.

Mythic: Morgana raised the undead remains of Roman soldiers for her army in the Shrouded Isles.
Folklore, not game canon: rowan (mountain ash) was planted in British and Irish churchyards and by doors as a charm against witches and the restless dead.

Caldey as Avalon's burying isle, the rowans that walk, the clan that came in the second summer, the payments of Little Haven, Mordwywr's ledger, the two Devmers and two Gorvoses and the harmless Telsar are Living Server writing; Hedd the ferryman and the counted lamps come from the Caer Sidi files.

story:
The burying isle. Caldey was where Avalon buried its dead. The colleges had their gardens on Avalon and their farms in the dales, and they sent their dead west over the water to the last isle before the open sea, where the priests of the dead kept the barrows and the graveyards and planted rowans round them, as the old custom is, to keep the dead lying down. Readers, fishermen, tenants and lords of the isles were carried there for longer than the colleges had kept count, and older dead were there before them: the barrows on the heights belonged to nobody the colleges could name. Out beyond the western strand, where no rock is, the turning gaol of Caer Sidi stood on the water, and the priests said the dead of Caldey had the shortest walk in the world.

What went wrong. When Morgana raised the dead of the isles, Caldey had more of them than all the other isles together. The garrison on the Isle of Glass says she did not need to work hard here. The isle stood up. The rowans that were planted to hold the dead down are haunted now and walk the south-western heights with the rest. The white lights that the priests carried at burials burn over the graves by the hundred with nobody carrying them. Phantom magi, the colleges' own dead readers, drift with the headless footmen and the grasping ghouls along the old burial road in the south, and dread liches and blood liches hold the northern ground towards the strand. In the marsh the dead have rotted into gangrenous masses. Not every priest of the dead resisted. Durval, who kept a barrow in the west, took Morgana's coming as the answer to his prayers.

The named of the isle. The oldest thing on Caldey is not dead at all: a winged serpent, the amphiptere, that roosts in the north of the isle and sheds its teeth when it is hurt, and where its teeth fall the ancient dead come up out of the ground. In the north-east Vortanos keeps a prison of the dead that only he can wake, and walks only by day. By the graveyard nearest Caer Sidi's door a crypt guardian keeps watch over a young sorceress of the colleges, Eralyne, who died on Caldey and was raised there and whose soul someone at Fort Gwyntell wants freed. Two dead men called Devmer walk the western slopes and two called Gorvos the eastern, and nobody has worked out whether they are four men or two. A guagaran called Palifan rules the stagnant pools in the middle of the isle. And among the dead of the south lives a thing called Telsar, a quiet jelly of the pools, which the fishermen say is the only creature on Caldey that has never harmed anybody.

Little Haven. The living hold one corner of the isle, on the north-eastern coast: the fishing village of Little Haven, whose people have always seen Caer Sidi from their doors and count its lamps, and beside it the outpost of a highland clan that came over the water after the war began to fight the dead where there were most of them. The clan keeps its own: a matron over all of them, maidens who sell shields and armour and instruments, a smith, a fletcher, a tailor, a leech, an enchanter, a bard who harms nobody, and barbarian defenders on the walls. The villagers pay for proof of the dead destroyed: Rose for shrouds, Tristram Adamson for skeletons' shin-bones, Huidelon Cariston for the hands of the pitch-dark dead, Waleron Douglas for the water-orbs of the drowned. Mordwywr, an enchanter of Albion, keeps the largest building in the village and asks for proof of seven kinds of dead at once.

Why it matters to Albion. Caldey is the door to Caer Sidi, and every company that goes into Arawn's gaol crosses this isle of the dead to reach the strand. It is also where most of Morgana's army came from. The clan says that while Caldey stands up, the witch will never run short of soldiers, and that every grave on the isle put back to sleep is one fewer at the Isle of Glass wall.
legend: Caldey is the high SI isle in the far west, levels 45 to 65, and the way to Caer Sidi: the entrance is in the north-west on the strand. It is almost all undead (Undead Servants of Morgana): white lights, phantom magi, headless footmen, grasping ghouls, liches, ancient zombies and haunted rowans, so bring cure disease and anything that is good against undead. Little Haven on the north-east coast is the only safe spot: Mordwywr there gives Malignant Creatures (kill seven kinds of undead), and the clan outpost next door has merchants, a smith and a healer, but your standing with the Caldey Outpost decides how friendly they are. The villagers Rose, Tristram Adamson, Huidelon Cariston and Waleron Douglas take undead turn-ins. Eralyne and the Crypt Guardian (59) are at the graveyard near the Caer Sidi door (Lost Treasure). Three catalog nameds: the Amphiptere (71) in the north near Little Haven, Durval (65) in his barrow in the west, Vortanos (61) in the north-east, who is untargetable at night. Each respawns about an hour after death.

book.title: The Ledger of Little Haven
pages: The Ledger of Little Haven, kept by Mordwywr, enchanter of Albion, in the largest building in the village, of what has been paid and to whom for proof of the dead put down. The villagers asked me to keep it because I can write and because, they said, an enchanter can tell a true bone from a false one. I can. Caldey was Avalon's burying isle. The colleges sent their dead here for longer than they kept count, and the priests planted rowans round the graves to keep them lying down. When the witch called, the isle stood up. The ledger is long.

Of the payments. Rose pays for shrouds, because she sewed half of them. Tristram Adamson pays for the shin-bones of the black skeletons; he says a skeleton without a shin does not walk to the wall, and he is right. Huidelon Cariston pays for the hands of the pitch-dark dead. Waleron Douglas pays for the water-orbs of the drowned, and will not say why, except that his brother went into the water. I pay for seven kinds at once, a kind from each of the isle's worst, so that the payer has walked the whole isle. The clan pays for nothing. The clan simply goes out.

Of the clan. A highland clan came over the water in the second summer of the war to fight the dead where there were most of them, and built its outpost by the village. Its matron decides who comes in. Its defenders keep the wall, its maidens sell shields and armour and instruments, and its bard plays in the evening for the living, which on Caldey is a rare audience. They are short with strangers who have given them reason. They have buried more of their own than the village has, in a corner of the outpost, and they did not plant rowans over them.

Of the strand. In the north-west the isle ends at the western strand, and Caer Sidi stands on the water beyond it where no rock is. The village counts its lamps, as the village always has; Hedd the ferryman keeps the count on his stick. Near the gaol's door is the graveyard where a young sorceress of the colleges, Eralyne, was buried and raised. A crypt guardian stands over her. A woman of Fort Gwyntell wants her soul set free, and I have entered that as a debt the isle owes, not a payment. It is the only debt in the book.

Of the named. North of the village the amphiptere roosts, the winged serpent that is older than the graves, and where its teeth fall the ancient dead come up. Durval the priest keeps his barrow in the west and never once raises his hand to anyone; he speaks, and that is enough. Vortanos keeps his prison of the dead in the north-east and is not there at night, so the clan goes by day. I have entered nothing against any of them yet. The ledger has a page kept for each, and the pages are blank.

Of the rest, and of Telsar. Devmer walks the western slopes and Gorvos the eastern, each of them twice, and the clan's bard has a song asking which of each is the real one. Palifan, a great guagaran, rules the stagnant pools. And among the dead of the burial road drifts Telsar, a jelly of the pools, which has never harmed anyone and which nobody on Caldey will touch. The fishermen say it was here before the graves and will be here after. I have given it a page in the ledger and written nothing on it either, out of respect.
